remaining wound length relative to the initial wound length calculated by the punch
diameter. These new quantifications are added to Fig. 2F and G.
8. Figure 3: more Ki67 indicates more proliferating cells – co-staining is required to
conclude the effect on keratinocytes. Additional staining of fibroblasts should be
included, at minimum.
Response: In Fig 3A, we used keratin 14(K14) to stain keratinocytes and αSMA as the
marker for fibroblasts. We quantified the Ki67-positive cells only in the migrating tongue
of the epidermis positive for K14 staining. In the revised figure, we changed Y-axis as %
Ki67+/K14+ keratinocyte/mm2 to be clearer.
9. The reproducibility is also an issue; mouse experiments have been replicated twice
only. Porcine model requires more wounds.
Response: We recognize the importance of reproducibility and have made efforts to
ensure consistency across our experiments. Breeding K5.Smad7 db/db mice is
challenging due to the infertility of homozygous db/db individuals. Therefore, generating
K5.Smad7 db/db mice required crossing K5.Smad7 transgenic mice with heterozygous
db (db/+) mice. Therefore, the mouse experiments using transgenic mice were bred with
multiple litters and repeated twice, and experiments were performed using littermate
controls. We have merged the results from two independent experiments in Fig. 1E in
the revised manuscript, which includes quantification from 6-15 mice per group. For
experiments involving db/db mice receiving protein treatments, we have added
independent repeats in Fig. 1K and Sup Fig. 2.
We acknowledge the limitation of few pigs with limited wounds per pig. The Yucatan
mini-pigs (27–30 kg) were first chemically treated to induce diabetes (mimicking Type I
diabetes in humans), then being screened to determine which ones had sustained high
blood glucose (because not all of them did) but were not severely ill (due to diabetic
complications) to be used for experiments. Based on IACUC allowable criteria, the
number of wounds is limited to 12 per pig, each 2cm in diameter. Because the clinical
care from the clinical veterinary team for these pigs and the associated costs are more
extensive than in normal pigs, and the latency from waiting for pigs to be ready to do
experiments was about a year, adding more pigs are both time- and cost-prohibitive.
Taken together, pig wounds can only be used to validate the relevance to human diabetic
wounds but are limited for in-depth research. We have acknowledged this limitation and
the rationale for a complementary approach including both porcine and mouse models
for the study in the Introduction.
10. Details such as type of dressing used for porcine wounds are not included; what
type of 3M film was used for murine wounds?
Response: For the porcine wounds, we used 3M Tegaderm film to cover each wound.
The specific details were put into the Supplemental Methods based on the journal’s
request.
11. Inhibition of NETosis is novel, however it lacks mechanistic insights.
Response: We thank the reviewer for recognizing the novelty of our findings regarding
the inhibition of NETosis by Tat-PYC-Smad7. The reviewer’s comment also highlights the
challenge of NETosis research field, i.e., the lack of knowledge about which signaling
pathways regulate NETosis, which would give us the leads to dive into Smad7-associated
mechanisms. Therefore, in the revised manuscript, we first examined if the observed
effect is a physiological or pharmacology mechanism. We knocked down endogenous
Smad7 in dHL60 neutrophils and found that PMA-induced and high glucose-induced
NETosis was increased with Smad7 knockdown (Fig. 5H-J), suggesting this is Smad7-
specific mechanism. Second, mechanistically, Smad7 effect on NETosis is not due to
blockade of TGFβ signaling (Sup Fig. 13). Instead, Tat-PYC-Smad7 blocks neutrophil
histone H3 citrullination (Fig. 6A-D) and reduces MPO activity (Fig. 6F). MPO is essential
for NETosis, as it translocates into the nucleus to promote chromatin unfolding and
decondensation (Dufrane et al., 2006, Thiam et al., 2020). In our revision, we performed
immunostaining and confocal imaging to examine the localization of MPO within
neutrophil granules versus the nucleus following PMA stimulation in Tat-PYC-Smad7-
treated dHL60 cells. Our results showed that Tat-PYC-Smad7 localized to the nucleus
of dHL60 cells, while MPO staining appeared consistent with granule localization
following PMA stimulation (Fig. 6G). Our data also showed that Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated
cells retained MPO within granule-like structures (Sup Fig. 15), suggesting that Tat-PYC-
Smad7 may interfere with the large-scale release of granule components, i.e., an early
and critical step during NETosis. These new findings have been added to Fig. 6G, Sup
Table 1, Sup Fig. 15 and Fig. 5F-J. Taken together, the mechanisms of Tat-PYC-Smad7
on neutrophil NETosis could involve reduced MPO enzymatic activity (Fig. 6F),
the reduction of MPO escape from the granules (Fig. 6G) which otherwise would potentially
initiate NETosis, as well as Tat-PYC-Smad7/MPO nuclear colocalization (Fig. 6G) that
potentially reduce MPO-induced chromatin decondensation during NETosis. We have
revised the manuscript accordingly to address the reviewer’s concerns. Finally, in our
revised discussion, we pointed out that our current findings warrant future independent
studies for NETosis mechanisms and the mechanisms of Smad7 in this process at the
cellular and molecular levels.
12. Figure S1: evidence of dermabond is visualy noticable, but selectively on db/db
wounds. This confounds wound healing.
Response: We did not use dermabond during the wound experiment. The "dermabond-
like" appearance observed in previous Sup. Fig 1 (Sup. Fig 3 in the revised manuscript)
in the Regranex-treated groups is actually due to the residual marks left by the application
of Regranex, which is an adhesive gel with high viscidity. In the revised manuscript, we
have added this explanation in figure legend to avoid confusion.
13. Figure S2: Requires detailed labeling to indicate what morphology is being referred
to as foam-like, as all three conditions show F4/80+ cells.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We have revised the label for
F4/80⁺ foam-like cells in previous Figure S2 (current Sup Fig. 4A in the revision). In
addition, since the staining intensity and cell size of F4/80⁺ foam-like cells are distinct
from other F4/80⁺ myeloid cell populations, we applied a mask to identify foam-like cells
and defined it using HSV thresholding (H: 4–36, S: 35–101, V: 158–218) to set the signal
intensity. Additionally, a minimum object size threshold of 15 pixels was used to define
cell size, utilizing the Count & Measure function in CellSense software (Olympus, version
2.3). This approach objectively distinguishes foam-like cells from the general F4/80⁺
myeloid cell population, as shown in Sup Fig. 4B. Based on this method, we quantified
F4/80⁺ foam-like cell objects in vehicle-, Regranex-, and Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated db/db
wounds, as presented in Sup Fig. 4C. We hope this revision sufficiently addresses the
reviewer’s concern.
14. Figure S5: The authors state that ECM remodeling is reflected in CD31 staining for
endothelial cells, this is not correct.
Response: We have corrected the figure legend for this careless mistake. CD31 staining
reflects angiogenesis, not ECM remodeling. This correction is now in the current Sup
Fig.7.
Reviewer #3:
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and
to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response: We are glad our manuscript provided this opportunity to the reviewer.
Reviewer #4:
Although good efficacy has been shown in animal models, the safety, efficacy, and
feasibility of TAT-PYC-SMAD7 in actual clinical applications still require further validation,
as there may be challenges in translation. While the study reveals the role of TAT-PYC-
SMAD7 in inhibiting neutrophil activity and NETosis, the exploration of its specific
molecular mechanisms remains insufficient and may require more experimental data to
support. Despite the use of various animal models, the relatively limited sample size may
affect the statistical significance and generalizability of the results, necessitating further
expansion of the sample size for validation.
Response: We hope that addition of substantial amount of data from animal experiments
and mechanistic studies of NETosis in the revised manuscript have addressed the
reviewer’s concerns. These have been highlighted in the revised manuscript and
specifically addressed in responses to other reviewers.
Reviewer #5
1. The data on TAT-PYC-Smad7 inhibiting PMA-induced NETosis is exciting. To connect
this observation back to diabetes, it would be important for the authors to validate the
impact of Smad7 on NETosis in more physiologically relevant situations such as when
NETosis is induced with high glucose. It would also be important to show that expressing
Smad7 in dHL60 cells prevents NETosis to rule out a potential side effect of the TAT-PYC-
Smad7 biologics (e.g. smaller size thus higher delivery in the nucleus than endogenous
Smad7).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and have conducted additional
experiments in which NETosis was induced by high-glucose conditions. Our results
confirm that Tat-PYC-Smad7 effectively inhibits NETosis under these conditions, further
supporting its relevance to diabetic wound healing. As the reviewer suggested, we also
performed Smad7 knockdown in dHL60 cells using siRNA targeting Smad7. We found
that reducing endogenous Smad7 expression significantly increased the susceptibility of
dHL60 cells to both PMA- and high-glucose-induced NETosis. Because endogenous
Smad7 is a nuclear protein, our finding indicates that the effect of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on
NETosis is specifically linked to the functions of Smad7 . These results and relevant
methods are present in Fig. 5F-J and Supplementary Methods.
2. Because NETs are described as networks of DNA with nuclear/cytotoxic proteins, the
authors should demonstrate that cytotoxic green labels NETs by showing that it
colocalizes with citH3 neutrophil elastase or MPO. The authors could immunostaining for
these markers at the end of the live imaging period. It would also be important to show
Zoomed images of figure 6D – at this resolution, readers cannot evaluate whether the
cytotoxic green signal is extracellular (e.g. occupies a larger area than the typical cell
area).
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive advice. We have performed
immunostaining for citH3, and MPO with DNA cytotoxic green labels and confirmed the
colocalization with the cytotoxic green signal induced by PMA (Sup Fig. 12). Additionally,
we have included zoomed images (Fig.5C in the revised manuscript) to provide a clearer
view, confirming that the cytotoxic signal is extracellular and occupies a larger area than
the typical cell size. These data are added in the revised manuscript.
3. Further, the authors propose that Smad7 directly binds to MPO in the nucleus thus
preventing its function in NETosis. Although MPO was shown to be important for NETosis,
it is still not clear how it mediates the process – for instance, MPO enzymatic activities
are not required for NETosis (https://doi.org/10.1083/jcb.201006052). Was the IP in figure
6H done with the nuclear fraction to show that MPO-Smad7 interaction occurs in the
nucleus? Did the author exclude the possibility that TAT-PYC-Smad could enter neutrophil
granules and prevent MPO from accessing the nucleus?
Immunostaining and confocal imaging could be used to assess MPO nuclear vs granules
localization after PMA stimulation of TAT-PYC-Smad7 treated dHL60 cells.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions. The IP was performed
using total cell lysates because Tat-PYC-Smad7 can travel between the cytoplasm and
the nucleus similar to endogenous Smad7. Following the reviewer’s advice, we conducted
immunostaining and confocal imaging to examine MPO localization in neutrophil granules
versus the nucleus following PMA stimulation in Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated dHL60 cells. We
found that without Tat-PYC-Smad7, MPO had more nuclear localization after PMA
stimulation (Sup Fig. 15). In contract, MPO is largely located in granules with the
presence of Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment. Confocal microscopy further revealed that
although colocalization of Tat-PYC-Smad7 with MPO occurred in nuclei of some dHL60
cells (yellow arrows in Fig. 6G), MPO positive granules did not have colocalization with
Tat-PYC-Smad7 (Fig. 6G). Therefore, our data suggest two potential mechanisms of
Tat-PYC-Smad7-mediated NETosis reduction. First, Tat-PYC-Smad7 treated cells
retained MPO within granule-like structures (Sup Fig. 15), raising the possibility that Tat-
PYC-Smad7 may interfere with the large-scale release of granule components — an early
and critical step during NETosis. Second, Tat-PYC-Smad7 could directly interact with
MPO once MPO enters the nucleus. Our data warrants future studies for the molecular
mechanisms governing granule content release during NETosis, and if and how this
process involves positive feedback loops where initial escape of granule contents
facilitates further release of NET components and promotes chromatin decondensation.
As the reviewer pointed out, the exact mechanisms by which MPO contributes to
NETosis are largely unknown and would warrant independent studies beyond the scope
of our current study. Given that MPO appears to have less escape from the granule
component and NET formation with the presence of Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment, it is
possible that Tat-PYC-Smad7 also targets an upstream step in NETosis, with the MPO
interaction contributing to — but not solely accounting for — its inhibitory effects.
We have added the new imaging data into Fig. 6G and Sup Fig. 15 and revised the
Discussion to soften our interpretation of the MPO–Tat-PYC-Smad7 interaction and
emphasize the need for future studies to dissect the detailed mechanisms underlying
these observations. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions, which have helped us
clarify and refine the mechanistic interpretation of our findings.
4. The authors show that TAT-PYC-Smad7 prevents citrullination of H3 in PMA treated
dHL60 cells without impacting the expression level of PAD4. This is an interesting dataset
that suggests that Smad7 is important for PAD4 enzymatic activity. First, for reproducibility
purposes, the authors should show and quantify repeats of the western blots shown in
figure 6 F and G. In vitro experiments testing the impact of smad7 on PAD4 citrullination
activity would be important to clarify how Smad7 prevents H3 citrullination and NETosis,
potentially independently of Smad7-MPO interaction.
Response: As the reviewer recommended, we have added data for western blot repeats
and quantified the results which are presented in the revised Fig. 6B and D. We sought
to investigate whether Tat-PYC-Smad7 directly modulates PAD4 enzymatic activity using
a commercially available PAD4 inhibitor assay. However, all commercial PAD4 activity kits
contain chemicals (not present in normal cells) interfering with the conformation of Tat-
PYC-Smad7 protein. As a result, within the technical limitations of the current assay
systems, we were unable to directly assess the impact of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on PAD4
enzymatic activity. We plan to explore this in future investigations when alternative assay
methods.
5. Finally, the author proposes that Tat-PYC-Smad7 prevents neutrophils degranulation.
Could the author please indicate which data supports this claim? The decreased release
of neutrophil elastase could also be due to the defects in NETosis since cells release
neutrophil elastase during NETosis.
Response: We agree that the reduced release of neutrophil elastase is more likely due
to impaired NETosis rather than direct inhibition of degranulation. We have revised the
manuscript to reflect this and removed the statement regarding the effects on neutrophil
degranulation.
6. This reviewer appreciates the difficulties of experimenting with animals. However, the
sample size of the pig dataset is very low. And some of the analysis is done with only Pig
1 in the main figure (Pig 2 and 3 are pulled in Sup fig.9 which shows a broad distribution)
where the authors perform statistical test (t-test) on samples with 4 data points. This low
sample size makes the t-test very unreliable. For example, in “figure 3, D)- TAT-PYC-
Smad7, 4ug” one data point is much higher than the 3 other data points which pulls the
mean % CD31+ area up – in such a small sample size, an outlier has a strong impact.
Another example of how the small sample size impacts the conclusion of the study is in
figure 5 D where the distribution of the %Ly6G+CitH3+ cells/area shows two populations
which alters the mean. This data set cannot be tested with a t-test which assumes a
gaussian distribution of the sample. Thus, the in vivo data (figure 3-C, B, D Fig 5 D and
E) requires more data points for the statistical tests used here and the conclusions of this
study to be meaningful. The authors should also show the standard deviation of their
distribution instead of the standard error of the mean (SEM), which does not allow readers
to appreciate the heterogeneity of the population.
Response: We acknowledge the reviewer’s concerns regarding the sample size in the
pig experiments. Given that the results of IHC/MSI quantification showed similar trends
for the three pigs, we merged the data from the three pigs for quantification to improve
the statistical integrity. Former Fig. 3D, E and Fig. 5E (Fig. 5B in the revised manuscript),
after merging the data from pig 1-3, we used ROUT method (Q = 1%) to identify the
outliers of the data. After eliminating the outliers from data, we used Shapiro-Wilk
normality test to detect the normality of the data. For the data sets fit the Gaussian
distribution, we used a two-trailed unpaired t-test for pairwise comparison between two
groups. For data that do not fit Gaussian distribution, we used the Mann-Whitney test for
pairwise comparison between two groups. For data from Fig. 5D (Fig. 5A in the revised
manuscript), we did a new set of staining using samples from another independent
experiment. We merged two data sets and did the same statistical processing as
described above. We have revised the manuscript to clearly state the limitations regarding
sample size for pig study and have updated the figures to present SD rather than SEM,
providing a more accurate reflection of data variability.
7. A big picture question that the authors might want to discuss is the potential side effects
of Tat-PYC-Smad7 biologics. If this biologic prevents neutrophil functions, and MPO
activity - which is important for host defense against microbes, will the application of Tat-
PYC-Smad7 enhance pathogen propagation at the wound site?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s important question regarding the potential side
effects of Tat-PYC-Smad7, particularly its impact on neutrophil function and host defense
against infections. In our animal models, we did not observe an increase in infection rates
following Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment in db/db mouse studies or pig studies. Additionally,
our data showed reduced infiltrating Ly6G+ neutrophils on day 11 but not on day 9 post-
treatment (Fig. 4E and F). This suggests that Tat-PYC-Smad7 does not affect neutrophil
recruitment during early stage of wound healing when host defense is more prominent.
Furthermore, Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment did not trigger any changes in CBC parameters
or little/effects on systemic cytokine levels (Sup Fig. 5), indicating that its functional
impact on neutrophils may be localized to the wound site and is likely limited to later
stages of wound healing.
Neverthelss, we agree with the reviewer that the effect of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on host
defense against microbes needs to be more comprehensively studied in the future. We
have revised the discussion section to highlight this limitation and point to future studies
to directly evaluate the safety and potential effects of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on neutrophil-
mediated antimicrobial responses.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-Point Response to Reviewers’ Comments
We sincerely appreciate that the editorial board has given us an opportunity to revise and
resubmit our manuscript. We are grateful for the thoughtful and constructive comments
from the reviewers. We have added more data to address reviewers’ concerns and
revised our manuscript based on reviewers’ comments and new data. Responses to
reviewer’s comments are provided below explaining how the concerns are addressed
experimentally and/or conceptually. In the revised manuscript, contents directly
addressing reviewers’ concerns are highlighted in yellow. We hope that our responses
have addressed all the reviewers’ concerns, and the revised manuscript is strengthened
significantly.
Critiques – Responses
Reviewer #1
1. First, concerning sample size and model validation: The persistent issue of small
sample sizes with apparent individual differences in Figures 1B and 1C significantly
undermines experimental reproducibility. We note the authors' explanation regarding
model construction difficulties, but these technical challenges do not alleviate concerns
about statistical power (In Fig1B and C, there are small samples of different numbers in
the same group. Originally, such small samples lack repeatability. The observed individual
variations necessitate re-evaluation of the model's reliability, as similarly highlighted by
Reviewers 2 and 4. 
Response: Fig. 1B and 1C consist of 4 genotypes in which most important comparisons
are between db/db and Smad7/db/db mice. We could not control equal distributions of
sex and genotypes during breeding to generate these bigenic mice (and it is noteworthy
that both strains are poor breeders). Therefore, previous data were from female mice
because K5.Smad7 genotype only had one male mouse. To make the data more
transparent, we included data from pooled sexes in the revised Fig. 1B and C and
included genotypes and sex in Sup Table 1. Each mouse’s genotype, sex, weight and
glucose can be found in the data source file. As you can see below, the revised figures
with more mice did not change the conclusion. Specifically, K5.Smad7/db/db mice (n =
10) showed reduced weight and glucose levels compared to db/db mice (n = 16), with a
subset of K5.Smad7/db/db mice even displaying glucose levels within the normal range.
This observation prompted us to include Tat-PYC-Smad7 topical treatment to the wounds
Previous Fig. 1B, 1C Revised Fig. 1B, 1C
in db/db mice to directly test whether the effect of Smad7 is systemic or primarily local in
promoting wound healing. Additionally, Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment to pig wounds included
vehicle controls in each pig in which systemic glucose and weight are the same. We hope
these three complementary experimental systems could convince the reviewer that
Smad7 effects are largely at the local/wound site.
2. The proposed regulation of MPO by Smad7 lacks comprehensive experimental
validation. While binding interactions are demonstrated, the precise regulatory
mechanism within the NETosis pathway (both upstream and downstream) remains largely
speculative (the author only discussed binding, and how Smad7 regulation/MPO is
affected in the upstream and downstream parts of NETosis is still mainly speculative). As
Reviewer 5 appropriately noted, the potential cytoplasmic regulation remains unverified,
representing a significant gap in the mechanistic framework.
Response: There are still significant gaps in the field’s understanding of the basic Netosis
mechanism itself (including both up- and downstream steps), which makes it challenging
to assess the step at which Smad7 acts. This fact does not diminish the novelty of the
observation that Smad7 inhibits NETosis. However, to further address the reviewer’s
concern and add mechanistic insight, we performed a new experiment including co-
staining of Lamin B1 (a nuclear membrane marker), MPO, HA, and DAPI in dHL60 cells
treated with Tat-PYC-Smad7 or vehicle control at early stages during PMA-induced
NETosis, to examine whether MPO colocalization with DNA and Smad7-HA occurs within
an intact nucleus or only after DNA release. The data have been added to the manuscript
as revised Fig. 6G. We find that during dHL60 cell stimulation with PMA, MPO enter the
nucleus in control cells by 1 hour, but it is often excluded from the nucleus in Tat-PYC-
Smad7-treated cells at the same time point. When colocalization with DNA and Smad7-
HA does occur, it is often detected within cells that retain an intact Lamin B1 ring. We
discuss these results and their mechanistic implications, but we have also tried to be
careful to avoid overinterpretation. We hope these data provide more insight into potential
mechanisms.
As Reviewer 5 noted, the precise mechanisms by which MPO contributes to NETosis
remain largely unknown and would warrant independent studies beyond the scope of this
work. Nevertheless, our study provides a novel mechanistic entry point by identifying
Smad7-MPO interactions and a role for Smad7 in opposing nuclear entry of MPO during
early stages of NETosis. These observations could guide future investigations as the field
advances. We have modified our Discussion section to describe these results and to
make it clear that there are important mechanistic gaps that will need to be resolved in
future studies.
3. Cited reviewer’s question and our response from rebuttal of NCOMMS-24-47156-R1:
“Question 2: A previous study has reported the feasibility of using exogenous Smad7
below an oncogenic level to alleviate skin inflammation and wound healing defects
associated with excessive activation of TGF-β and NF-κB. In my view, the ideas of this
study coincide to some extent with those of this previous study. In addition, Tat-PYC-
Smad7 reduced neutrophil infiltration and attenuated TGF-β and NFκB signaling
pathways were also reported (PMID: 34610386). It is necessary to add and highlight the
discussion about the innovation points of this study.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s comment that we should more clearly delineate
conceptual innovations and novel findings of the current study compared to our previously
published studies. In the revised discussion, we have clarified the novelty of the current
study: in addition to providing direct evidence (compared to previous correlative studies)
that Smad7-based therapeutic effects target TGFβ and NFκB in two diabetic wound
models, we identified that the effect of Smad7 on neutrophil activity, specifically on
NETosis, which is independent of TGFβ signaling. This effect is difficult to capture in other
experimental model systems in which neutrophil infiltrations are often transient.”
Reviewer’s comment regarding the cited content in Question 2: We recognize the relevant
elaboration but still feel that it lacks strong persuasiveness.
Response: Unlike our earlier proof-of-concept work, here we directly test Smad7 in bona
fide diabetic wound models using both preclinical mouse and pig systems, establishing
its therapeutic potential in clinically relevant contexts. Importantly, we identify a new
mechanism, the suppression of excessive NETosis, which extends beyond previously
reported effects and provides translationally significant insights into diabetic wound
pathology. We have revised the Introduction and Discussion to emphasize these
innovations more explicitly.
4. Question 4-1：Our concerns about the fourth part are not unnecessary. First of all,
the diabetic mouse model should have elevated blood glucose concentration for a long
time (for more than 4 weeks). The significance in Fig1B and Fig1C is to demonstrate the
role of Smad7 in wound healing. However, we found that in the K5Smad7/db/db mice,
there was a group of mice whose blood glucose levels fluctuated abnormally. Should this
mouse be regarded as having individual differences? And just as several other reviewers
were concerned, we believe that a small sample size makes it difficult to determine
causal relationships and is accidental. We do not deny that Smad7 has a good effect in regulating
NETosis, but blood glucose level is also an important indicator of wound healing,
even though it has been verified in later articles. However, it is hoped that this phenomenon of
blood sugar fluctuations can be explained to support the errors caused by too few animal
experiments.
Response: We would like to clarify that the db/db mice indeed have lifetime high glucose,
we only showed the data encompassing our experimental period. As the reviewer noticed,
K5.Smad7/db/db mice showed significantly lower weight and glucose levels and this
holds true even with additional pooled mouse data (revised Fig. 1B and 1C). For this
reason, we generated a Tat-PYC-Smad7 protein to test its treatment efficiency on diabetic
wound via topical application. We found that topical treatment did not affect glucose or
body weight observed in the transgenic model yet still promoted healing, indicating that
the Smad7 effect is mainly at the local wound site. As the reviewer indicated, high glucose
in db/db mice contribute to NETosis, and topical Smad7 in this high glucose condition still
has effects. These data do not contradict but rather support reviewer’s point.
5. Question 4-2：Furthermore, regarding the animal part, the wound healing images
presented by the db/db group in Fig1D show almost no visual difference, but there is a
significant wound healing effect during the statistical process. We believe that, like other
animal experiments, a scale or control substances should be added. Therefore, it is hoped
that the author can adjust the zoom ratio of the pictures and place the scale ruler to
enhance the readability of the article.
Response: We greatly appreciate that the reviewer identified the deficiency for our data
presentation and provided this excellent suggestion. In the revised Fig.1D, we have
calibrated and adjusted the zoom ratio, added scale bars, and selected more
representative images that are consistent with the quantitative wound healing results. We
believe these changes improve the readability of the figures and better reflect the
statistical outcomes.
Reviewer #2
The authors have improved mechanistic aspects focused on NETosis, however multiple
issues remain.
1. Fig 1L, not clear what blue lines represent, please clarify.
Response: In Fig. 1L, the blue lines indicate the leading edge of the migrating epidermal
tongue, identified by reduced collagen density and the absence of hair follicles as
visualized by H&E staining. We have added this clarification into the corresponding figure
legend.
2. Fig 2D, the area selected to show epidermal wound edge in the Smad7 treated
wounds is questionable as epidermis appears as crust, quantification of K14 staining
would be more appropriate than h&e
Response: In the revised Fig.2D, we have shown the enlarged image with higher
resolution to show the epidermal wound edge is not the crust. We also added the K14
staining of the skin sections to show the consistency of the epidermis shown in H&E.
3. Quantification of CD31/angiogenesis in porcine wounds is questionable as it is
expressed as "objects per migrating epithelium" (Fig 3). Detailed CD31 quantification
requires area of cd31+ blood vessels per mm2 of the wound bed, regardless of
epithelialization.
Response: We apologize for not describing our quantification clearly. The vessels were
indeed quantified as per mm2 of the wound bed (see the square boxes) as recommended
by this reviewer, but we chose the area directly underneath the migrating epithelium.
Because angiogenesis at the leading edge is essential for wound closure, providing
vascular support that directly correlates with re-epithelialization, we simply used the
migrating epidermal length as a reference. In the revised manuscript, we have revised
the Y-axis from previous “/mm2 migrating epithelium” to “/mm2 wound bed underneath
migrating epidermis” to make it clear.
4. -a-sma is diminished in Smad7-treated murine wounds (fig 3a), while this is not
surprising it may impact the quality of scar tissue, please quantify and discuss.
Response: We have added the quantification of the a-sma in Vehicle and Tat-PYC-
Smad7-treated wounds in revised Fig.3A and add the result in the Results and
Discussion sections.
5. The area selected as representative for elastic fibers in a pig wound day 16 is
questionable as well, as it does not focus on the wound bed, it shows unwounded area.
Response: The representative image of elastic fibers at Day 16 was selected to illustrate
the transition zone adjacent to the wound margin, where remodeling of elastic fibers
occurs as part of re-epithelialization and matrix deposition. Our intent is to highlight
changes at the interface between wounded and unwounded tissue, rather than in the
intact dermis. We have revised the figure legend to specify that the image depicts the
wound margin area. In addition, we have added images closer to the wound margin area
to confirm that the observed elastic fiber alterations are consistent across the wound area
in the revised Fig.3F.
6. Significant number of genes regulated at the later time point, day 11, suggests
regulation of processes beyond the neutrophil function, the most active phase of
neutrophils during wound healing is between days 3-5, please comment.
Response: To address the reviewer’s comment, we have added Ly6G staining on days
3 and 5 of the db/db wounds in the Sup. Fig. 9B. These analyses revealed only sparse
neutrophil infiltration in the wound beds, which is consistent with previous reports showing
that diabetic conditions impair neutrophil chemotaxis and delay their recruitment to the
wound site (Roy et al., 2022). This explains why a larger number of genes appear
regulated at the later time point (day 11), when neutrophil activity remains detectable in
db/db wounds compared with the more transient peak typically observed between day 3-
5 in normal wound healing.
7. RNAseq data and manuscript overall would be significantly improved by comparative
transcriptional analyses from generated RNAseq post-Smad7 treatment and the publicly
available datasets from human diabetic foot ulcers.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. After surveying available
resources, we found that datasets from interventional clinical trials on diabetic foot ulcers
are very limited. We identified one project (GSE269483) in the Gene Expression Omnibus
database that included 10 human samples in a treatment setting; however, the treatment
outcomes were not disclosed, which prevents meaningful comparison with our study. At
present, we are not aware of publicly accessible datasets that would allow us to evaluate
treatment effects in a way that could be directly aligned with our Smad7 work. Moreover,
existing human diabetic foot ulcer datasets are highly heterogeneous, reflecting
differences in ulcer stage, infection status, anatomical site, diabetes duration, and patient
comorbidities. These factors make it challenging to draw parallels with the controlled,
time-matched wound healing experiments performed in our mouse model. For these
reasons, we are not able to include a reliable data-mining analysis at this stage.
8. In fig 5b, CitH3/MPO staining enlargement of vehicle and tat-pyc-Smad7 treated
porcine wounds is mostly focused on the "crust" area which often results in unspecific
staining in the porcine wound model. It is not clear why authors do not focus on the actual
wound bed area with significant CitH3 signal. Similarly in murine wounds area above
epidermis is zoomed in for the vehicle treated wounds, while wound bed is zoomed in for
the tat-pyc-Smad7 treated wounds (Fig 5a)
Response: We focused on the crust/surface region because NETs typically accumulate
at the wound surface where neutrophils release extracellular traps into the exudate, as
reported in cutaneous wound studies (Zhu et al., 2021). To ensure specificity, only
CitH3/MPO/DNA co-localized structures were quantified. For clarity, we have revised Fig.
5 to include matched regions from both the surface crust and underlying wound bed. We
have added this data in the revised Fig. 5A and B.
Reviewer #3:
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and
to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response: We are glad our manuscript provided this opportunity to the reviewer.
Reviewer #5
1. While the role of smad7 in preventing NETosis is convincing, the molecular
mechanisms lack strong supportive data. The confocal images in Sup figure 11, 12, 15
have limited resolution / are blurry, which makes it hard to assess MPO granular versus
nuclear localization. The data currently in the manuscript shows that MPO colocalize with
DNA and smad7-HA (Figure 6, Zoom), but whether this localization occurs inside an intact
nucleus or after DNA is released from the nucleus is not clear. I strongly suggest the
authors clarify this in the manuscript so that follow up studies can rigorously address the
question of when and where Smad 7 /MPO interaction occurs.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the need to clarify whether MPO
colocalization with DNA and Smad7-HA occurs inside an intact nucleus or only after DNA
release. To address this, we performed additional immunofluorescence experiments with
Lamin B1 (a nuclear membrane marker), MPO, HA, and DAPI co-staining.
This new data is presented in revised Fig.6G. It shows that in the presence of Tat-
PYC-Smad7, MPO is mostly excluded from the nucleus at 1 hour. In contrast, we also
see cells in which MPO has entered the nucleus, and we observe colocalization of MPO
with DNA and Tat-PYC-Smad7-HA within a continuous Lamin B1 ring, indicating that the
nuclear envelope remains at least largely intact at this stage. While we cannot fully rule
out subtle nuclear alterations, these results suggest that MPO nuclear entry and its
colocalization with DNA and Tat-PYC-Smad7-HA occur prior to overt disruption of the
nuclear membrane. We have revised the manuscript in the Results and Discussion
sections to include this clarification.
2. Figure 5I: It could be helpful to readers to see zoomed images as in Figure 5F.
Response: In the revised figure, we have added zoomed-in panels for Figure 5I, similar
to Figure 5F, to provide clearer visualization and enhance readability for the readers.
3. Figure 6B: Please indicate on the figure panel that B quantifies CitH3. How is B
normalized? From panel 6A, it looks like CitH3 is highest at 30 min but the graph shows
comparable values. The authors could consider normalizing relative to the first time point
to show how CitH3 levels change over time after PMA stimulation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In the revised figure, we have
indicated in the panel label that Fig.6B quantifies CitH3. The grayscale intensity of protein
bands was quantified using ImageJ software. Each band was normalized to its
corresponding loading control, and the resulting values were further adjusted relative to
the highest intensity band, which was set to 1. The statistical analysis was performed
using data from three independent experiments. We have described the quantification
method in the supplementary method. The apparent stronger CitH3 signal at 30 min in
the blot of Figure 6A appears less distinct in the graph because of this normalization
approach as the background density in the other two lanes are relatively stronger as well.
We tried to normalize the citH3 value to the first time point but found that this approach
would not reflect the differences between the treatment groups.
3. Figure 6C: Interesting to note that no CitH3 was detected in cells treated with 3 ug of
TAT-PYC-Smad7 while this amount of the biologics minimally impairs NETosis based on
figure 5.
Response: In Figure 6C, cell lysates were collected only at 30 minutes after PMA
treatment, whereas in Figure 5 we performed longitudinal observations. The inhibitory
effect of low-dose Tat-PYC-Smad7 may become less pronounced over time compared to
higher doses. Nevertheless, as shown in Figure 5D, even the low-dose Tat-PYC-Smad7
treatment produced a statistically significant reduction in NETosis.
4. Figure 6E: How long after PMA stimulation? does it match with a limited co-localization
observed in 6G?
Response: The data in Figure 6E (Sup. Fig. 15 in revised manuscript) were collected 1
hour after PMA stimulation, consistent with the early stage of NETosis shown in the
revised Fig.6G. At this timepoint, we see limited NETosis but we do see MPO
colocalization with Tat-PYC-Smad7-HA in the nuclei of some cells. This biochemical
approach supports an interaction between Smad7 and MPO, although the imaging results
are more informative for where the interaction is occurring.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: Reviewer：The authors have commendably addressed all the raised concerns with substantial revisions. To enhance the robustness of the in vivo data, they have increased the sample size and re-evaluated the relevant parameters. Furthermore, they provided further validation of blood glucose levels in the knockout mice, effectively clarifying this issue. Building on this, they systematically verified the therapeutic effect of the target gene through both local injection and systemic administration in diabetic mice. Finally, to substantiate the involvement of NETosis, the authors incorporated new staining experiments and convincingly demonstrated its correlation with wound healing outcomes.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: Congratulations to the authors for the revisions. My major questions are answered and the manuscript should be published, in my opinion.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_6: This study is well-designed and highly significant, exploring a Smad7-based protein agent (Tat-PYC-Smad7) for diabetic wound healing. While the reviewers rightly noted that the mechanism linking Tat-PYC-Smad7 and MPO needs more work, we agree with the authors' statement that fully elucidating this may require a new, systematic study. For now, the authors have adequately addressed the points raised by Reviewer 2. The study doesn’t just confirm Smad7’s known role in blocking the TGFβ/NFκB pathway—it also shows that Smad7 directly inhibits neutrophil NETosis. However, neutrophils play a dual role in wound healing, being crucial for clearing pathogens. Although this research doesn’t cover infection, real-world diabetic wounds are frequently infected. We believe this is worth keeping in mind, as it could potentially influence the future clinical application of Tat-PYC-Smad7.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Diabetic wounds have limited effective therapies to restore tissue repair and resolve
excessive inflammation. This study aimed to identify mechanisms of diabetic wound
healing defects and test a therapeutic intervention using diabetic mouse and pig models.
Here we show that Smad7 transgene expression in mouse epidermis promotes wound
healing in diabetic mice. To restrict therapeutic effects of Smad7 on wounds, we develop
a Smad7-based biologic (Tat-PYC-Smad7) that penetrates cells of the wound. Topical
Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment to diabetic pig and mouse wounds accelerates healing. Tat-
PYC-Smad7-treated wounds exhibit reduced TGFβ/NFκB signaling, faster re-
epithelialization and better extracellular matrix remodeling compared to vehicle controls.
Tat-PYC-Smad7 also attenuates neutrophil ext racellular trap (NET) formation, potentially
acting through reductions in MPO enzymatic activity and MPO nuclear entry,
consequently reducing chromatin Ldecondensation and the release of NET components.
Our study reveals that keratinocytes and neutrophils are the two major cell types targeted
by Tat-PYC-Smad7 to pRromote diabetic wound healing, providing insight into mechanisms
of diabetic wound healing defects targetable by Smad7-based therapy.

## Introduction

Impaired wound healing in diabetes represents a significant cause of morbidity 1.
Standard wound management is often ineffective, posing global health, economic, and
social issues 2, 3. Becaplermin/Regranex, a recombinant platelet-derived growth factor
(PDGF)-BB, is the only FDA-approved topical drug for diabetic foot ulcers 4. However,
Regranex requires large, repetitive doses to achieve modest improvement in a small
proportion of patients 5. In addition, long-term use of growth factors is linked to a
carcinogenesis risk 6. Hence, developing novel, effective treatments for diabetic wounds
is an unmet medical need.

The wound healing process includes stages of inflammation, proliferation, and
remodeling 3. In diabetic wounds, healing stal ls at the inflammation phase 7. One of the
hallmarks of nonhealing human wounds is keratinocyte dysfunction 8, which has been
considered a therapeutic targetL for diabetic wounds9. Prolonged inflammation in
nonhealing wounds generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to keratinocyte
injury, apoptosis, and imRpaired migration 10. Moreover, altered extracellular matrix (ECM)
composition and enhanced ECM degradation by elevated matrix metalloproteinase levels
in nonhealing wounds impair keratinocyte attachment, leading to aberrant cell signaling
and impaired survival and migration 11. In addition to keratinocyte dysfunction, prolonged
infiltration and activation of inflammatory cells, mainly neutrophils, are the main source of
proinflammatory cytokines, proteases, and ROS in chronic wounds 12, and contributes to
the recruitment of more immune cells, alterations in the proteolytic balance, and impaired
blood vessel formation 13. Collectively, keratinocyte dysfunction, sustained neutrophil-
driven inflammation, proteolytic imbalance, and impaired angiogenesis delay wound
healing, exacerbate scar formation, and predispose local lesions to neoplastic
progression 7, 14. In patients with diabetes, elevated glucose levels promote neutrophil
extracellular trap (NET) formation through the process of NETosis 15. The pathogenic role
of prolonged neutrophil activity in diabetic wounds potentially serves as a therapeutic
target. Conversely, individuals with neutropenia or those suffering from conditions with
neutrophil abnormalities (such as deficiencies in adhesion or neutrophil granules, etc.)
are more susceptible to wound infections resulting in abnormal wound healing processes
16. The impaired wound healing observed in neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction
suggests that a systemic approach to targeting neutrophils may not be viable because
neutrophils play dual roles in wound healing.

To study mechanisms of healing defects in diabetic wounds and test therapeutic
interventions, animal models have been dev eloped 17. Excisional wounds in diabetic
BKS.Cg-Dock7m +/+ Leprdb/J (db/db) mice have a significant healing delay, with
reductions in neovascularization aLnd epidermal proliferation 18. Miniature diabetic pigs
are also a model for wound healing studies due to the similarities of their skin texture to
humans 19. While theR diabetic porcine model offers a clinically relevant model, e.g.
enabling an assessment of treatment effects on ECM remodeling, its limitations, such as
the extensive clinical care, long preparation time, and limited excisional wounds per pig
restrict its feasibility for mechanistic investigations. Therefore, mouse models provide a
complementary resource for mechanistic studies. We previously observed that transgenic
mice constitutively overexpressing wild-type TGFβ1 in keratinocytes (K5.TGFβ1wt) with
TGFβ/NFκB signaling activation exhibited a significant delay in full-thickness wound
healing, characterized by profound inflammation, keratinocyte apoptosis, and ECM
dysregulation 20, 21. We also found that TGFβ and NFκB are activated in human diabetic
wounds 21, suggesting that a TGFβ/NFκB dual inhibitor, Smad7, may have therapeutic
effects on diabetic wounds. Smad7 consists of an N-terminal and C-terminal domain, with
a linker region containing a PY motif 22. The functional activities of Smad7, including
blocking TGFβ/NFκB signaling, are attributed to its C-terminal domain and PY motif 23.
These domains of human Smad7 share 99% amino acid homology with mouse and pig
Smad7, enabling the use of these animal models to investigate its function while
minimizing species-mismatch-associated immunogenic responses 22. In this study, we
employed both genetic and pharmaceutical models to assess the role of Smad7 in
diabetic wound repair. We provide evidence that Smad7-based proteins promotes
diabetic wound healing via supporting epithelial cell survival, ECM modification, and
attenuating adverse neutrophil activities.

## Results

K5.Smad7 transgene expression and Tat-PYC-Smad7 topical application mitigated
wound healing defects of db/db mice.
We previously developed K5.Smad7 mice, which express Smad7 in keratinocytes 24. We
bred K5.Smad7 mice with db/db mice that have obesity and type 2 diabetes 25, to
generate K5.Smad7/db/db bigenic mice. Grossly, K5.Smad7/db/db mice had sparse hair
(Fig.1a), similar to K5.Smad7 mice 26. The db/db phenotype of obesity and high blood
glucose levels were significantly lower in K5.Smad7/db/db mice than in db/db littermates
(Fig.1b-c, Supplementary Table 1). Microscopically, K5.Smad7/db/db skin showed mild
epidermal hyperplasia and hypertrophic sebaceous glands, similar to K5.Smad7 skin
(Fig.1a). To assess whether the K5.Smad7 t ransgene could attenuate wound healing
defects of db/db mice, we established excisional wounds by skin punch (6mm) on the
dorsal skin of mice and observeLd wound healing kinetics. Compared to db/db mice,
wound healing in K5.Smad7/db/db mice was significantly accelerated from day 9 to day
11 (Fig.1d-e).

Because K5.Smad7 mice expressed Smad7 transgene in other epithelial cells in addition
to keratinocytes 24, to assess whether Smad7 healing is a direct effect on wounds or a
secondary effect of attenuated diabetic phenotype or from other tissues, we generated a
Tat-PYC-Smad7 protein that contains the functional domains of human Smad7 with a cell-
penetrating Tat peptide. An optional HA tag was added to the C-terminus of Tat-PYC-
Smad7 enabling tracking of this exogenous protein (Fig.1f). Testing topical application of
Tat-PYC-Smad7 on normal mouse skin wounds indicated a relatively long stability of Tat-
PYC-Smad7 (at least 12h) (Fig.1g). Four full-thickness skin wounds were induced using
a skin punch on the dorsum of mice on day 1, followed by topical treatment every other
day and covered by a 3M film after treatment (Fig.1h). Tat-PYC-Smad7 penetrated both
epithelial and stromal cells of db/db wounds (Fig.1i). Grossly, we observed accelerated
wound healing in both K5.Smad7/db/db wounds and wounds of db/db mice treated with
Tat-PYC-Smad7 from day 9 to day 11 (Fig.1j-k). Histologically, K5.Smad7 transgene
expression or Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment led to increased diabetic wound healing rates
(Fig.1l-m). Additionally, there was a reduction in the remaining wound length and an
increase in the length of the epidermal migrating tongue in K5.Smad7/db/db wounds and
Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated wounds, compared to vehicle-treated db/db wounds (Fig.1l, n,
o). Notably, Tat-PYC-Smad7 topical treatment exerted an effect comparable to K5.Smad7
transgene expression in promoting diabetic wound healing. We did not observe a
significant change in either blood glucose or b ody weight in mouse hosts with Tat-PYC-
Smad7-treated wounds compared to the vehicle control (Supplementary Fig.1).

We found a dose-dependent eLffect of Tat-PYC-Smad7 in accelerating wound healing
(Supplementary Fig.2). Then we used 1µg of Tat-PYC-Smad7, which showed the best
treatment efficacy, Rto compare with standard-of-care treatment, Regranex
(Supplementary Fig.3a). Tat-PYC-Smad7 significantly expedited wound closure
compared to either vehicle or Regranex treatment on day 5 and 7 (and comparable
healing to Regranex at later time points) and Tat-PYC-Smad7 had an overall higher rate
of healing (Supplementary Fig.3b-e). From day 8 to day 11, wounds treated with Tat-PYC-
Smad7 exhibited reduced size and longer lengths of epidermal migrating tongues
compared to vehicle (similar or better than Regranex-treated wounds) (Supplementary
Fig.3f-h). We also observed foam-like F4/80+ myeloid cells in Regranex-treated wounds
but not in Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated wounds (Supplementary Fig.4). These foam-like cells
with internalized lipids and a characteristic foamy cytoplasmic appearance may indicate
active inflammation and have been linked to a profibrotic phenotype 27. Regranex-treated
mice had increased numbers of circulating white blood cells including lymphocytes,
monocytes, and granulocytes compared to vehicle- or Tat-PYC-Smad7 treated mice
(Supplementary Fig.5a). In addition, Regranex, but not Tat-PYC-Smad7, upregulated
pro-inflammatory factors such as Angiopoietin 2, chemokines CXCL16 and CXCL5, LDL
receptor (LDL R) and IGFBP3 (Supplementary Fig.5b and c).

Tat-PYC-Smad7 promoted the healing of diabetic pig wounds.
To assess the effect of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on wounds closely mimicking human skin, we
used three miniature diabetic pigs and punched twelve 2cm diameter full-thickness
wounds in each pig for drug treatment (Fig.2a). Two doses of Tat-PYC-Smad7 protein (2
µg and 4 µg) or vehicle control of either hydro xypropyl cellulose (HPC) or hydroxyethyl
cellulose (HEC) were topically applied every other day and wounds were covered with a
medical dressing (Fig.2a). ImmunLohistochemistry staining for Smad7 revealed that Tat-
PYC-Smad7 was detected in the epidermis and stromal cells at the wound edge in
protein-treated woundsR, while it was absent in vehicle-treated wounds (Supplementary
Fig.6a). To assess whether topically applied Tat-PYC-Smad7 enters the bloodstream, a
Smad7-specific ELISA was developed, capable of detecting levels as low as 5 ng/mL.
Smad7 remained undetectable in systemic circulation in all treated pigs (Supplementary
Fig.6b). We evaluated whether Tat-PYC-Smad7 induced an anti-drug antibody (ADA)
response that could neutralize its therapeutic effects and found no detectable ADA against
Tat-PYC-Smad7 in treated pigs (Supplementary. Fig 6c). Wound healing kinetics among
individual pigs varied, resembling variations in human diabetic wounds 28, hence wound
healing response to treatment of each pig by gross evaluation was analyzed individually.
Grossly, the treatment effects of Tat-PYC-Smad7 became evident from day 8, 5 and 11
for pig 1, 2 and 3, respectively (Fig.2b-c). Histological analysis indicated that more than
30% of the wounds were healed in the Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated group compared to 8%
of the vehicle group (Fig.2d-e). Tat-PYC-Smad7 significantly reduced the remaining
wound length as a percentage of the initial wound length compared to the vehicle control,
indicating enhanced wound closure in diabetic pigs (Fig.2f). Moreover, Tat-PYC-Smad7
treatment resulted in longer epidermal migrating tongues in all three pigs compared to
vehicle controls (Fig.2g).

To understand the pathogenic targets of Tat-PYC-Smad7 in wound healing, we
performed immunofluorescent staining of diabetic pig and db/db mouse wound sections
and found that Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated wounds contain more Ki67+ cells and less αSMA+
area compared to vehicle-treated wounds (F ig.3a-b, Supplementary Fig.7, suggesting
increased keratinocyte proliferation and less fibrotic response. Moreover, Tat-PYC-
Smad7 restored angiogenesis in thLe stroma area under the migrated epidermis in diabetic
pig wounds and db/db mouse wounds, with more CD31-positive areas at the edge of Tat-
PYC-Smad7-treated wRounds compared to control wounds (Fig.3c-d, Supplementary
Fig.7b). Additionally, Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated wounds had more regenerative and
organized wavy elastic fibers (stained as black to blue/black striae) entwined among
collagenous fibers shown by Pentachrome staining in healed wounds of db/db mice on
day 25 and diabetic pig wounds on day 16 (Fig.3e-f), indicating that Tat-PYC-Smad7
improved ECM deposition and collagen remodeling.

To understand the molecular basis of Tat-PYC-Smad7 effects, we performed RNA-
seq on db/db mouse wound samples excised at identical locations treated with vehicle or
Tat-PYC-Smad7 on days 9 and 11. Days 9 and 11 are critical stages at which db/db
wounds start to transition towards a chronic state, compared to normal wounds 18.
Principal components analysis revealed distinct transcriptomic profiles of Tat-PYC-
Smad7-treated wounds vs vehicle-treated wounds (Fig.4a). The number of differentially
expressed genes (DEGs) was 211 on day 9 and 612 on day 11, with 72 DEGs overlapping
between the two timepoints (Fig.4b). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the
Hallmark gene sets showed that Tat-PYC-Smad7 inhibited TGFβ and NFκB signaling,
inflammatory responses and apoptosis pathways (Fig.4c and Supplementary Fig.8),
consistent with known TGFβ/NFkB effects on wound healing in our previous reports 21, 29
as well as phenotypic changes seen in Fig.3a-b. Interestingly, enrichment analysis using
the overlapping DEGs between day 9 and day 11 on gene ontology (GO) terms identified
that neutrophil functions affected by Tat-PYC-Smad7 were among three out of top five
enriched biological processes (Fig.4d). As DEG enrichment analysis indicated a
significant impact of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on neutrophils on both day 9 and day 11, we
examined Ly6G+ neutrophils in theL wound beds and found that the number of Ly6G+ cells
was unchanged by Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment on day 9, but significantly reduced on day
11 (Fig.4e-f), suggestinRg that Tat-PYC-Smad7 may affect neutrophil functionality and
chemotaxis. Analysis of wound tissue lysates from day 11 using an antibody array
revealed that wounds from mice treated with Tat-PYC-Smad7 had reduced
proinflammatory proteins and cytokines, including CXCL5 30, lipocalin2 31, and cytokine
IL33 32, and granule components myeloperoxidase (MPO) 33 and Pentraxin 3 34,
compared to wounds from mice treated with vehicle (Fig.4g-h). Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated
wounds also had decreased elastase production on day 11(Fig.4i), which is often
associated with neutrophil degranulation or NETosis 35. Therefore, Tat-PYC-Smad7 exerts
effects on both epidermis and stroma cells in diabetic wounds with better healing
outcomes.

Tat-PYC-Smad7 blunted neutrophil activities in diabetic wounds at molecular and
cellular levels.
In addition to the impact of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on keratinocytes and ECM regulation, GSEA
of GO terms on day 9 and day 11 showed the top 3 functional clusters associated with
neutrophil activities that were consistently attenuated by Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment
(Fig.4j, Supplementary Fig.9a). This is consistent with the later-stage neutrophil infiltration
observed in db/db mouse wounds, as Ly6G staining showed only sparse neutrophil
presence on days 3 and 5 in comparison to abundant neutrophil infiltration on day 9 and
day 11 after wounding (Supplementary Fig. 9b). Immunohistochemistry staining of the
wound tissues showed penetration of Tat-PYC-Smad7 in both keratinocytes and Ly6G+
cells in protein-treated wounds (Supplementary Fig.10), indicating a possible direct effect
of Tat-PYC-Smad7 on neutrophil functions. Additionally, in diabetes, high glucose (HG)
levels induce neutrophils to undeLrgo NETosis 15. Neutrophils recruited to wound sites
almost immediately undergo NETosis and complete NET release in ~2.5 hours 15. To
evaluate the Tat-PYC-SRmad7 effect on NETosis in vivo, we examined a transcriptomic
profile of NETosis 36 previously demonstrated to be specifically involved in diabetic wound
healing defects 15. We found that the NETosis-related gene set was downregulated in
wounds treated with Tat-PYC-Smad7 (Fig.4k and l), with similarly strong enrichment as
other neutrophil-associated gene sets (Fig.4j and Supplementary Fig.9a). Furthermore,
in both diabetic pig and db/db mouse models, immunofluorescence staining indicated
fewer neutrophils undergoing NETosis in the Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated wound beds,
determined by co-staining of Ly6G or MPO (neutrophil markers) and citrullinated histone
3 (citH3) (NETosis marker) with DAPI (DNA marker) (Fig.5a-b). These data suggest that
Tat-PYC-Smad7 blunts neutrophil NETosis in diabetic wounds.

Tat-PYC-Smad7 prevented PMA and high glucose-induced NETosis in dHL60 cells.
To test if Tat-PYC-Smad7 directly affects NETosis, we performed an in vitro assay using
phorbol myristate acetate (PMA)-induced NETosis in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-
differentiated HL60 cells (dHL60), a neutrophil cell culture model 37. Tat-PYC-Smad7-HA
was detected in the nucleus 5min after treatment, showing highly efficient cell penetration
(Supplementary Fig.11a). We observed that dHL60 cells treated with Tat-PYC-Smad7 had
fewer cells marked with NETs 4 hours post-induction with PMA (Supplementary Fig.11b).
Live cell imaging using IncuCyte showed significant attenuation of PMA-induced NETosis
by Tat-PYC-Smad7 in a dose and time-dependent manner (Fig.5c-d). Cytotoxic Green, a
cell-impermeant DNA dye that labels extracellular DNA released during loss of membrane
integrity, colocalized with citH3-positive neutr ophils and MPO in PMA-induced dHL60
cells (Supplementary Fig. 12), confirming that the observed signal represented NETosis.
We also observed reduced elastasLe release from dHL60 cells 4 hours after PMA induction
following Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment, an additional marker of NETosis (Fig.5e). NETosis
induced by HG, mimickiRng the blood glucose levels in diabetic wounds, was also inhibited
by Tat-PYC-Smad7, (Fig.5f-g). Furthermore, siRNA knockdown of endogenous Smad7 in
dHL60 cells significantly increased NETosis under both PMA- and HG-induced conditions
(Fig.5h-j), suggesting Smad7 suppresses NETosis. PMA-induced NETosis was not
affected by BSA, TGFβ or TGFβ inhibitor treatments (Supplementary Fig.13), suggesting
attenuation of NETosis by Tat-PYC-Smad7 was not related to its effect of antagonizing
TGFβ signaling or as a non-specific protein.

We next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the effect of Tat-PYC-Smad7
on neutrophil activity. As histone citrullination is the critical step for NETosis 38, we first
investigated whether Tat-PYC-Smad7 affects this process. PMA-induced citrullinated
histone 3 (citH3) was blocked by Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment at all time points examined
(Fig.6a-b) and all doses of Tat-PYC-Smad7 blocked citrullination of histone 3 (Fig.6c-d).
PAD4, the key enzyme for histone citrullination 38, showed no significant change in protein
levels following Tat-PYC-Smad7 treatment (Fig.6c-d). We conducted a pulldown assay
with a Smad7 antibody recognizing Tat-PYC-Smad7 using lysates of PMA-treated dHL60
cells treated with the vehicle or Tat-PYC-Smad7. Mass spectrometry analysis showed
several proteins were enriched in Tat-PYC-Smad7 samples pulled down with anti-Smad7
antibody (Supplementary Fig.14a-b). A list of the top Tat-PYC-Smad7-binding targets
includes MPO (Supplementary Fig.14b), a protein required for NETosis via translocation
into the nucleus to promote chromatin unfolding 38, 39. Consistent with mass spectrometry
findings, MPO was detectable in anti-Smad 7 pulldown samples only from Tat-PYC-
Smad7/PMA-treated dHL60 cell lysates, supporting a potential interaction between Tat-
PYC-Smad7 and MPO (Fig.6e)L. Functional assays revealed that Tat-PYC-Smad7
treatment attenuated both peroxidation and chlorination activities of MPO under NETosis
condition (Fig.6f), whichR contribute to NETosis through reactive oxidant generation, lipid
peroxidation, and chromatin remodeling 40. To further investigate the impact of Tat-PYC-
Smad7 on MPO dynamics during NETosis, we performed immunofluorescence co-
staining with MPO, HA-tagged Tat-PYC-Smad7 and Lamin B1 (a nuclear membrane
marker). MPO enters the nucleus 1 hour post-PMA treatment in the vehicle condition, but
MPO is largely excluded from the nucleus in the Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated cells at this
timepoint (Fig. 6g). By 2.5 hours, Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated cells still showed reduced
nuclear MPO accumulation and extracellular spread of MPO compared with vehicle
control (Fig. 6g). We also observed instances where MPO entered the nucleus of treated
cells, where it colocalized with DNA (DAPI) and Tat-PYC-Smad7-HA within a continuous
Lamin B1 ring at 1 hour and 2.5 hours of PMA-induced NETosis (Fig. 6g). Consistently,
at 2.5 hours, colocalization between Tat-PYC-Smad7 with MPO appeared mainly in MPO-
positive nuclei in Tat-PYC-Smad7-treated and PMA-stimulated dHL60 cells
(Supplementary Fig.15). Colocalization analysis showed that about 20-30% of the strong
HA and MPO signals appeared in the same locations, based on thresholded Manders’
coefficients. The thresholded Pearson’s correlation coefficient (Rcoloc) was close to +1,
indicating that HA and MPO signals were strongly associated in signal-rich regions
(Supplementary Table 2).
